title: AI Unlocked: Christian Ministry
blurb: For pastors, elders, missionaries, and ministry teams: a biblically grounded theology of technology, sermon and Bible-study preparation with integrity, the ministry tool landscape compared, discipleship and communication at scale — and an unflinching module on what must remain human. Anchored in Scripture and in John Lennox’s 2084.

modules.t: Imago Dei & the Machines: A Theology of Technology
modules.d: What Scripture says about human uniqueness — and why AI makes it urgent.
modules.body:
Start where the Bible starts

"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him" (Genesis 1:27). Every AI debate — consciousness, personhood, work, worth — eventually collides with this verse. Machines predict; humans bear the image of God. That distinction is the foundation of this entire course.

The Lennox framework

Oxford mathematician John Lennox, in 2084: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Humanity, gives the church its clearest map: take AI's real capabilities seriously, refuse both panic and worship, and test every transhumanist promise against the gospel's actual answer to death and human upgrading — resurrection in Christ, not silicon. As Lennox reminds audiences, "Nonsense remains nonsense, even when talked by world-famous scientists" — a caution that cuts both ways: against AI hype, and against dismissing it unexamined.

A biblical pattern for technology

  • Creation mandate: tools extend our stewardship of the garden (Genesis 1:28, 2:15) — the plow, the codex, the printing press, the language model.
  • Babel warning: technology amplifies the heart behind it (Genesis 11) — capability without submission to God builds towers, not temples.
  • Wisdom test: "Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord" (Colossians 3:23) — the question is never only can we, but for whom.
"Man's power over Nature turns out to be a power exercised by some men over other men." — C.S. Lewis, The Abolition of Man (1943). Lewis saw the AI governance debate eighty years early: every "powerful tool" question is really a "who wields it over whom" question.

Where the secular consensus agrees with us

Remarkably, the world's ethics bodies have landed near biblical ground: UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of AI — the first global standard, adopted by 193 states — centers "human rights and human dignity" and insists on human oversight of machines. The church has been saying "human dignity" since Genesis 1. This module equips you to say it with fluency in both vocabularies.

Reflection assignment: write a one-page answer to a church member who asks "Should Christians fear AI?" — using Genesis 1:27, one Lennox argument, and one honest acknowledgment of real risk. Bring it to mentor office hours.

modules.t: Sermon & Bible Study Preparation with Integrity
modules.d: Exegesis support, illustration mining, series design — and the pulpit integrity rule.
modules.body:
The preparation stack

  • Original-language study: "Act as a Greek professor. Walk me through the grammar of Philippians 2:5–11 clause by clause; flag every translation decision and what hangs on it." Then verify against your trusted lexicons and commentaries — AI is a study partner, not an authority.
  • Historical-cultural context: first-century background briefs, checked against scholarly sources.
  • Illustration engine: "Give me 5 contemporary illustrations of costly grace for a congregation of [profile]" — then supply your own lived story; borrowed authenticity preaches hollow.
  • Series architecture: an 8-week expository arc through a book: big idea per text, discussion questions, memory verses, and a children's-track version of every week.
  • Accessibility: the same sermon rendered as a plain-language summary, a youth devotional, and a French translation — one input, a whole congregation served.

The pulpit integrity rule

AI may organize your study; it must never replace your encounter with the text. "Study to shew thyself approved unto God… rightly dividing the word of truth" (2 Timothy 2:15) is addressed to you. Our house standard: every AI-assisted step documented, every quotation verified, and the sermon preached is one you own before God. Many pastors add a public norm ("our teaching team uses AI for research support, never for the message itself") — you will draft yours in the capstone.

🧪 Interactive Lab — run this now

You are a seminary-trained research assistant serving an evangelical pastor. For [passage], produce: (1) a verse-by-verse exegetical outline with original-language notes, (2) three cross-references with one sentence on the connection, (3) two illustrations for a mixed congregation, (4) five small-group discussion questions, and (5) a list of every claim I must verify in commentaries before preaching. Passage: [enter yours].

opts: AI organizes study; the preached message is yours before God

modules.t: Tool Study: The Ministry Technology Landscape
modules.d: Logos AI vs general LLMs vs church platforms — compared for doctrine-sensitivity, cost, and fit.
modules.body:
Comparative snapshot (verify current tiers — this market moves)

  • Logos Bible Software + AI features: the deepest study library with AI-assisted search and summarization across YOUR trusted books; subscription tiers from student to scholar; strongest choice for expository ministries — AI grounded in vetted theological sources rather than the open internet.
  • General LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini): unmatched flexibility for drafting, translation, admin, and study dialogue — but doctrinally ungrounded: they will fluently summarize heresy and orthodoxy with equal confidence. Rule: doctrinal claims get verified in Scripture and your confession, every time.
  • Church management platforms (Planning Center, Tithe.ly, Subsplash-class): scheduling, giving, check-in, and follow-up automation with AI features arriving; priced per campus/size; the administrative backbone.
  • Media stack: Canva (bulletins, sermon graphics), CapCut (sermon clips for youth reach), NotebookLM (turn your own sermon archive into small-group guides and even a discussion-style audio recap), Suno (worship-adjacent audio for announcements — with your worship leaders' discernment on what belongs in gathered worship).

Selection criteria for a church budget

  • Doctrine-sensitivity of outputs · data privacy for member information · total cost per month vs volunteer hours saved · bilingual capability · does it serve the 80-year-old member as well as the 18-year-old?
Access paths: solo pastors → free LLM tiers + Canva free + NotebookLM (all $0) cover 80% of this course. Established churches → Logos subscription + one management platform. Denominations → negotiate multi-church licensing.
🧪 Interactive Lab

Act as a church technology consultant with deep respect for biblical ministry. Our church: [size, budget/month, staff count, languages, current tools]. Recommend a complete ministry technology stack in three tiers (free / modest / full), with monthly costs, the volunteer-hours each tool saves, and one risk per tool I should manage. Format as a table.

modules.d: Small groups, follow-up, missions, and the multilingual church.
modules.body:
The Great Commission has a logistics layer

"Go ye therefore, and teach all nations" (Matthew 28:19). Teaching all nations involves translation, materials, follow-up, and coordination — exactly what AI accelerates. The Word doesn't change; the paper-shuffling around it can shrink dramatically.

Workflows

  • Small-group engine: every sermon auto-becomes a leader's guide (summary, 5 questions from observation to application, prayer prompts) — NotebookLM on your own manuscript keeps it faithful to what was actually preached.
  • Newcomer pathway: automated but warm — welcome message, what-to-expect guide, pastor's follow-up reminder at day 3 (your Make/Zapier skills from the No-Code Builder Lab).
  • Discipleship tracks: a 40-day new-believer devotional drafted from your church's teaching, reviewed by elders, delivered daily by broadcast list.
  • Bilingual congregation: every bulletin, announcement, and study guide in English and French from one input — the Cameroonian church's reality, and increasingly every church's.
  • Missions support: field updates → prayer letters; supporter communication; culture-and-language briefs for short-term teams (verified with your field workers).

The guardrail

Discipleship is relationship. AI schedules the coffee; it doesn't have it. Metrics worth tracking: hours returned to actual pastoral contact per week — that number is this module's fruit.

🧪 Interactive Lab

Here is my sermon manuscript: [paste]. Produce: (1) a one-page small-group leader guide with 5 questions moving from observation to application, (2) a 5-day family devotional from the same text, (3) a 60-word midweek encouragement message for our broadcast list, and (4) all three in French. Preserve my exact doctrinal emphases; flag anywhere you were tempted to soften or alter them.

modules.t: What Must Remain Human — and Answering the Age
modules.d: Pastoral care, prayer, and discernment; plus AI apologetics for your congregation.
modules.body:
The non-delegable core

  • Pastoral counseling, crisis presence, confession, deathbeds: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Romans 12:15) — weeping cannot be automated. AI may help you prepare resources; it never responds in your place.
  • Prayer: a chatbot can draft a liturgy; it cannot intercede. Guard the difference fiercely, and teach your people to.
  • Confidences: what is shared in pastoral confidence never enters an AI tool. Ever. Not anonymized, not summarized. This is a bright line.
  • "AI Jesus" chatbots and grief-bots: understand the ache they answer — loneliness, loss — and offer the church's better answer: embodied community and living hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

AI apologetics: your congregation is already asking

Equip yourself for the questions arriving in your foyer: Can a machine have a soul? (Consciousness and the imago Dei — Lennox's central chapters.) Will AI take my job — where is God in that? (Vocation, provision, and the church's practical response: this academy exists partly to answer that.) Is AI the beast/Babel/the end? (Sober eschatology: watchfulness without date-setting, Matthew 24:36.) Should my teenager use AI for homework? (Integrity formation — the Education specialization's playbook, discipled.)

Lennox's counsel throughout 2084: the Christian response to AI is neither fear nor worship, but discipleship — because the future belongs to the risen Christ, not to the machines. UNESCO can regulate systems; only the gospel addresses the heart that builds them.
plAIbox™: prepare and deliver (to your cohort) a 10-minute congregational talk: "A Christian's Guide to AI" — one Scripture, one Lennox insight, one practical household rule, one hope. Peer-reviewed for warmth and accuracy.

modules.d: A working system, a public charter, and elder-ready governance.
modules.body:
Capstone requirements

  • One month of documented practice: AI-assisted sermon prep logs, the discipleship engine running, and time-returned-to-people metrics.
  • Your Ministry AI Charter (one page, public): what we use AI for; what we never delegate (preaching, prayer, pastoral care, confidences); our verification standard for doctrine; our disclosure norm to the congregation.
  • Elder briefing: a 10-minute presentation as if to your elder board or church council — costs, benefits, guardrails, and the biblical rationale.
  • The apologetics talk from Module 5, refined.
"And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Colossians 3:23). Graduates receive the AI Unlocked: Christian Ministry certificate. Natural next steps: the Servant Leadership Accelerator (#LeadLikeJesus) or AI for NGOs for church-based community work.
